prompt.context: Robot & Company (Robot Co.) is a company headquartered in California, USA and Shenzhen, China, the two important world capitals for hardware innovation. In early 2020 catering has undergone significant change, especially with the breakout of Covid-19. Robot Co. is catching up the market trend with the rollout of Gundam-II, a robot specifically designed to deliver dishes and drinks from the kitchen to the dining area. The robot executes orders in the system instantly and disinfects itself at the end of each mission (disinfection takes 5 seconds). The CEO of Robot Co. has tasked us with figuring out whether to launch Gundam-II in Singapore, and how to price this new product.
prompt.question: Should Robot Co. launch Gundam-II in Singapore, and if so, how should they price the product?

clarifying_info.q: Where are Robot Co.'s operations located?
clarifying_info.a: R&D is in California and Shenzhen; manufacturing is in Shenzhen; sales network covers North America, North Asia, and Southeast Asia.
Gundam-II is patented and Robot Co. has strong technical leadership. No potential competitors are expected in the foreseeable 2-5 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the business model — sell or lease?
clarifying_info.a: Robot Co. plans to lease Gundam-II to restaurants for a monthly rental payment, not sell outright.
No-contact service has become the new norm post-Covid, reducing virus transmission risk and helping management cut labor costs.

exhibits.title: Dimension of Gundam-II at Full Capacity vs. Dimension of Super Drink
exhibits.shows: A diagram showing the internal loading dimensions of Gundam-II and the outer packaging dimensions of Super Drink (a popular drink in Singapore restaurants).
exhibits.data: Gundam-II max loadable volume: 20 x 21 x 35 inches. Super Drink outer packaging: 5 x 7 x 4 inches.

exhibits.title: Single Task Efficiency of Gundam-II vs. Server
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of task-by-task time for Gundam-II versus a human server to serve a standard meal for 4 customers.
exhibits.data: Pick up dishes & beverages: Gundam-II 1.5 min x 1 time; Server 2 min x 4 times. Deliver dishes & beverages: Gundam-II 2.5 min x 1 time; Server 1.5 min x 4 times. Place dishes & beverages: Gundam-II 1 min x 4 times; Server 1 min x 4 times. Total: Gundam-II 8 min; Server 16 min.

framework: Assess market attractiveness: size of Singapore restaurant market, demand for no-contact service, labor cost environment
Evaluate competitive position: Gundam-II patents, 2-5 year lead, no near-term competitors
Determine pricing approach: cost-based floor vs. value-based ceiling; lease model implications
Estimate market size at proposed price point
Identify key risks and mitigants before entering

questions.prompt: Question 1: With the full capacity of Gundam-II (20x21x35 inches), what is the maximum number of Super Drink packages (5x7x4 inches) that can be transported at one time? Gundam-II can adjust the orientation of packages.
questions.guidance: This is a spatial reasoning puzzle. The candidate must try all orientation combinations. The common wrong answer is 102 — the correct answer is 105. Key insight: by rotating the Super Drink package, a more efficient packing can be achieved on one axis.

math.setup: Gundam-II interior: 20 x 21 x 35 inches. Super Drink package: 5 x 7 x 4 inches. We can orient the drink package in any direction. Try different orientations across the three axes.
steps: Orientation A (5x7x4 along 20x21x35): floor(20/5)=4, floor(21/7)=3, floor(35/4)=8 → 4x3x8=96
Orientation B (5x4x7 along 20x21x35): floor(20/5)=4, floor(21/4)=5, floor(35/7)=5 → 4x5x5=100
Orientation C (7x5x4 along 20x21x35): floor(20/7)=2, floor(21/5)=4, floor(35/4)=8 → 2x4x8=64
Orientation D (7x4x5 along 20x21x35): floor(20/7)=2, floor(21/4)=5, floor(35/5)=7 → 2x5x7=70
Orientation E (4x5x7 along 20x21x35): floor(20/4)=5, floor(21/5)=4, floor(35/7)=5 → 5x4x5=100
Orientation F (4x7x5 along 20x21x35): floor(20/4)=5, floor(21/7)=3, floor(35/5)=7 → 5x3x7=105
Best orientation: 4x7x5 inches placed into 20x21x35 gives 5x3x7 = 105 units.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Robot Co. plans to rent out Gundam-II with monthly rental payments. How should they price the service? What factors should be considered?
questions.guidance: Candidate should address both cost-based floor and value-based pricing. Key factors: (1) cost of the robot amortized monthly plus maintenance, (2) value created for the restaurant — labor savings from replacing servers, adjusted for efficiency and shift coverage. Strong candidates will recognize the 24-hour vs. 8-hour shift advantage of robots. Because Robot Co. has no competitors for 2-5 years, value-based pricing is preferred. The exact price is an open question but must be justified.

math.setup: Cost side: Manufacturing cost SGD 9,000; lifespan 5 years; monthly maintenance SGD 100. Value side: server monthly salary SGD 1,600; Gundam-II is 2x as efficient per task (8 min vs 16 min); restaurants open 12 hours, servers work 8-hour shifts so 1.5 shift factor; Gundam-II replaces 80% of server functions.
steps: Monthly cost floor: SGD 9,000 / (12 months x 5 years) + SGD 100 = SGD 150 + SGD 100 = SGD 250/month
Value created per robot per month: SGD 1,600 x (16 min / 8 min efficiency ratio) x 1.5 shift factor x 80% replaceable = SGD 1,600 x 2 x 1.5 x 0.8 = SGD 3,840/month

Value-based pricing range: between SGD 250 (cost floor) and SGD 3,840 (full value). Given strong market position, a rental price capturing significant share of value created is justified (e.g., SGD 1,000–2,000/month).
math.answer: Cost floor: SGD 250/month. Value ceiling: SGD 3,840/month. Value-based pricing recommended given strong competitive moat.

questions.prompt: Question 3: If Robot Co. charges SGD 1,000/month per robot, estimate the annual market size of Gundam-II in Singapore. What numbers do you need and what are your key assumptions?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the key unknowns (number of restaurants, servers per restaurant, opening hours) before calculating. Key assumption is the percentage of restaurants willing to adopt robot service — candidate should provide rationale (luxury restaurants may not adopt, etc.). Strong candidates will clearly articulate the formula before plugging in numbers.

math.setup: Numbers needed: number of full-service restaurants (4,000), servers per restaurant (15), opening hours (12 hrs/day). Key assumptions: all restaurants same size; 70% willing to convert (rationale: high-service/luxury restaurants unlikely to adopt). Formula: restaurants x servers/restaurant x replaceable % / shift factor / efficiency factor x adoption rate x monthly rental x 12 months.
steps: Robots needed per restaurant: 15 servers x 80% replaceable / 1.5 shift factor / 2 efficiency factor = 15 x 0.8 / 1.5 / 2 = 4 robots per restaurant
Total addressable robots: 4,000 restaurants x 4 robots x 70% willing to convert = 11,200 robots
Annual market size: 11,200 robots x SGD 1,000/month x 12 months = SGD 134,400,000
math.answer: Annual market size: approximately SGD 134.4 million

questions.prompt: Question 4: What are the key risks Robot Co. should consider before entering the Singapore market, and how can they mitigate these risks?
questions.guidance: This is an open brainstorm. Candidate should organize risks into clear categories with mitigations. Three main categories: (1) Regulatory risks — food safety regulations, robot-in-public-space approvals, liability; (2) Gundam-II operational risks — technical failures, maintenance downtime, food contamination during malfunction; (3) Public perception risks — customer comfort with robot service, staff resistance/job displacement concerns, media/PR risk. Great candidates proactively identify risks without prompting.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks Robot Co. should consider when entering Singapore, and how can they be mitigated?

categories.name: Regulatory risks
ideas: Singapore food hygiene regulations may require additional certification for robot-assisted food service
Robots operating in public spaces may face licensing requirements from authorities
Liability for food contamination or accidents caused by Gundam-II needs legal clarity
Data privacy regulations if the robot has sensors/cameras recording dining areas

categories.name: Gundam-II operational risks
ideas: Mechanical failures during service leading to dropped dishes or spills
Downtime for maintenance reducing restaurant efficiency
Edge cases (unusual table layouts, crowded environments) that reduce robot performance
Battery life or charging logistics during 12-hour operating windows
Disinfection process (5 seconds per mission) may create bottlenecks in high-volume periods

categories.name: Public perception risks
ideas: Customer discomfort or negative experience with robot service, especially in fine dining
Resistance from existing restaurant staff fearing job displacement
Negative press coverage around robot failures or hygiene incidents
Cultural preference for human interaction in certain restaurant segments (luxury, family-style)
Restaurants concerned about brand dilution by appearing overly automated

recommendation: Robot Co. should enter the Singapore market given strong market demand post-Covid, a 2-5 year competitive moat from Gundam-II patents, and substantial value creation for restaurant clients
Adopt a value-based pricing strategy with monthly rental in the SGD 1,000–2,000 range, well above cost floor (SGD 250) but sharing meaningful savings with restaurant operators to drive adoption
Target mid-tier full-service restaurants first; avoid luxury segment where human service is a differentiating feature
risks: Regulatory approval delays could slow rollout
Operational failures in early deployments could damage brand reputation
Slower-than-expected restaurant adoption if economic conditions worsen
next_steps: Conduct regulatory pre-clearance with Singapore authorities before full launch
Run a controlled pilot with 3–5 restaurants to validate operational performance and gather NPS data
Develop tiered pricing or trial rental periods to lower adoption barriers for hesitant restaurant operators
